body: Wednesday, February 25 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: Policy is on hold while the trade rules are unsettled. Headlines disagree on the new global tariff: one says it started at 10% with the administration working to lift it to 15%, another says it went into effect at 10%, not the 15% that had been threatened. The Fed’s split is open. Goolsbee calls for a hold on cuts because inflation is ‘not good enough’, Bostic says the Fed cannot offset a possible rise in structural unemployment, and Waller does not expect AI to blow up the job market. The S&P 500 closed at 6,890.07, up 0.77% in the prior session but 0.87% lower over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), and the VIX fell 6.95% to 19.55 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Consumer confidence improved in February, but the cloud over the labour market remains.

Rates & Curve: The US Treasury par curve at the prior close shows the 2Y at 3.43% and the 10Y at 4.04%, a 10Y-2Y spread of 61 bps, a 10Y-3M spread of 35 bps and a 30Y yield of 4.70% (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-24). Over 20 observations the 2Y fell 13 bps from 3.56% and the 10Y fell 18 bps from 4.22%, so the 10Y-2Y spread narrowed by 5 bps, while the 3M is 2 bps higher over the same window. The curve is moderately steep, approaching the long-run average, and the 20-observation move is a bull flattening, with both yields down and the 10Y down more. Over the last five observations the 2Y is unchanged and the 10Y is 1 bp lower (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-24). The rally is stalling near 4%: Bloomberg reports the Treasury rally has stalled with the 10-year approaching 4%, and CNBC says the 10-year is little changed as markets weigh the tariff escalation. The DXY is at 97.88, up 0.87% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

New / Most Important: Two stories set the tone. The first is software. Stocks rebounded after Anthropic announced new partnerships, but Reuters says investors are still looking for signs of a bottom in the software rout, and Bloomberg says investors are dumping software stocks and earnings will not stop it. The second is private credit. The WSJ reports new benchmarks to pierce the opaque market, a private-credit fund is selling $477 million of assets at 94% of value, UBS sees defaults reaching 15% in its worst case, and Boaz Weinstein warns the wheels are coming off some private-credit funds. Jamie Dimon’s doubts about the credit market are described as well founded by Bloomberg.

Playbook ✓: Keep duration in the belly rather than chasing the long end. IEF is at 97.42, up 1.38% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), and the curve is bull-flattening. Trim software exposure into the bounce, because the rebound rests on partnership headlines rather than on earnings. Stay underweight private-credit lenders and business-development exposure until the new benchmark data are published, and keep a VIX hedge, since the index is still up 21.05% over 20 sessions even after falling in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The call changes if the 10Y moves back above its 20-observation-earlier level of 4.22% and stays there (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-24), which would mean the bull flattening is over, or if Nvidia’s report later today lifts the AI complex.

Macro Stance: Euro-area manufacturing is recovering while the trade calendar breaks down. Euro-zone business activity improved as manufacturing bounced back, and German manufacturing grew for the first time since 2022. The trade relationship is the risk. Bloomberg reports the EU is set to halt approval of the US trade deal, EU lawmakers have again postponed the vote, and a top trade lawmaker says the US has breached the deal and Europe is ready to retaliate. EUR/USD is at 1.1794, down 0.7% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Stance: Mixed, because the data are improving while the trade risk is rising.

Credit & Inflation: Banking supervision is tightening and inflation is coming down faster than forecast. The ECB has stepped up scrutiny of European banks’ AI-industry exposure, and Lagarde is under fire over an additional BIS salary. Panetta says Chinese imports helped drive a sharper-than-forecast inflation drop. German consumer sentiment darkened unexpectedly heading into March, while Irish consumer sentiment edged up to an 11-month high. Equity markets are near the top of their range: the STOXX Europe 600 closed at 629.14, up 2.61% over 20 sessions and 1.26% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), and the Euro Stoxx 50 is at 6,116.60, up 2.04% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

New / Most Important: The US trade friction is now the euro-area story. The EU is set to halt its approval, the Parliament has put the deal on ice, and the EU’s trade chief has said a deal is a deal, accepting no increase in US tariffs after the Supreme Court ruling. Merz travels to China with the economy on the line, and German auto exports to China plunged by a third in 2025, which means the German auto heartland is falling on hard times. A Reuters poll has Europe’s strong start to the year likely to peter out.

Playbook ✓: Stay neutral on the index and prefer the STOXX 600 over single-country beta while the trade vote is frozen, since the index is up 2.61% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Stay underweight German-exposed autos: the iShares autos ETF is only 2.95% higher over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), and Stellantis dealers in Europe are pushing for EU relief as sales lag. The call changes if the Parliament reschedules the vote and approves the deal, which would make the exporters a buy, or if the US adds sector tariffs that the EU has to answer.

Macro Stance: The Spring Festival gave a consumer read that beat the gloom. China’s longest Lunar New Year holiday lifted travel spending, and holiday travel boomed in a sign of a consumer sentiment rebound, although the festival box office has plunged to a six-year low. The People’s Bank has left benchmark lending rates unchanged for a ninth straight month. Stance: Mixed. The holiday data are a consumer bounce, while credit and property are still soft and the policy bias has not changed.

PMIs & Activity: The feed carries no new official manufacturing or services PMI in this window, so the activity read is the holiday data. Xinhua says Spring Festival consumption is injecting momentum into the global economy, and the festival box office reached 5.75 billion yuan. What would confirm the view is the next official PMI staying near 50, which is not in the feed, and holiday spending holding up once trading and factory activity resume.

Credit Impulse: The feed carries no fresh monthly credit print. The rate line is unchanged for a ninth straight month, and the EXIM Bank has over $289 billion of outstanding Belt and Road loans. Capital Economics says the investment-led growth era is ending. The credit impulse would show first in monthly loan data and in infrastructure approvals, neither of which is in the feed, so the view rests on the rate line and the property data.

Property: Property policy is easing at the margin. Shanghai is easing homebuying rules in its latest property relief, Hong Kong home sales are heading for a 22-year high, and mainland new home prices extended their decline as weak demand hit the sector. Commercial property is the weak spot: empty shops and falling rents in the retail slump, and The Economist describes the tail of the property bust as rotten.

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Beijing is retaliating in its Japan dispute. China imposed export controls on 20 Japanese entities and restricted exports to 40 Japanese entities with military ties, including Mitsubishi Heavy. On the US side, China says it will decide on tariff countermeasures in due course, and analysts think the court ruling points to steadier US-China ties before an April summit. Copper jumped as China traders cheered the prospect of lower US levies, which is a trade-relief signal rather than a growth gauge.

Markets & Flows: The Hang Seng closed at 26,590.32, down 1.82% in the prior session and 0.15% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The Shanghai Composite closed at 4,117.41 on 2026-02-24, up 0.87% in the prior session and 0.08% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), after the holiday break. The CSI 300 ETF ASHR is at 34.14, up 1.31% over 20 sessions, while the internet ETF KWEB is down 9.97% over 20 sessions at 32.25 and the large-cap ETF FXI is down 2.74% at 38.37 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). USD/CNY is at 6.9080, 0.66% lower over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). US investors have increased buying of Hong Kong and mainland Chinese stocks.

New / Most Important: Asia’s currency story is the one to watch. Asian currencies hit a 16-month high on the weak dollar and a stronger yuan, and Hong Kong is seeking more borrowers in an offshore yuan push. In equities the split is in tech. Reuters’ Morning Bid says Asian tech is blowing its own AI bubble, and the SCMP asks why the Hang Seng Tech Index is underperforming while AI shares soar. The AI rotation within China is still running: Chinese AI startups surged after the holiday in a rotation from big tech.

Playbook ✓: Buy the offshore yuan and policy-relief names selectively and avoid the internet ETF until it stops falling: KWEB is down 9.97% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Hedge with FXI, and keep mainland exposure to the holiday consumer names until a PMI print confirms the rebound. The call changes if the Trump-Xi summit is confirmed for April with a tariff framework, or if the countermeasures become a formal list. ⚠ Divergence: the Shanghai Composite is up on the holiday reopening while the Hang Seng fell 1.82% in the prior session, so the onshore and offshore tapes disagree (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

Macro Stance: The BOJ story has turned political. Mainichi reports that Prime Minister Takaichi voiced concerns about further rate hikes, and the government surprised the market by tapping two reflationists for the BOJ board. The yen extended its decline on the report. Services inflation is steady and signals wage-driven price pressure, which is the case for the BOJ not to fall behind. Stance: Mixed. The board appointments argue for a slower hike path, while services inflation argues against the delay.

Activity & Currency: USD/JPY is at 154.6, up 0.67% over five sessions and 0.19% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The Nikkei 225 closed at 57,321.09, up 0.87% in the prior session and 6.45% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Goldman says Japan’s blistering stock rally is not over, and Reuters’ poll sees the Nikkei breaching 60,000 by mid-2027 on earnings growth and foreign inflows. The yen is also tied to the US: the US led January’s yen rate checks, eyeing joint intervention with Japan. Japan is also squeezed diplomatically: China restricted exports to 40 Japanese entities with ties to the military, which is a second source of pressure on the corporate outlook.

Playbook ✓: Own the Nikkei with a partial yen hedge, not unhedged: the index is up 6.45% over 20 sessions while the yen is weak against the dollar near 154.6 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Prefer exporters while USD/JPY holds near that level, and keep domestic-demand names small until core inflation turns. The call changes if the BOJ signals a March move, which would strengthen the yen and hit the exporters, or if US intervention becomes a formal joint action.

Macro Stance: The RBA is back in focus. Australia’s core inflation hit a 16-month high and raised bets on a May rate hike, and Commonwealth Bank and Westpac have raised their own rates, which increases the chance of another RBA hike. The RBA published a speech on recent inflation developments and the economic outlook. Tariffs are the offset: Australia is described as the quiet loser from Trump’s new 15% tariff, and Labor called the tariffs unjustified as the ASX braced for a fall. Stance: Mixed, with a tightening bias and a trade drag.

Demand & Financing: AUD/USD is at 0.7061, down 0.71% in the prior session and up 2.11% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The S&P/ASX 200 closed at 9,022.30, down 0.04% in the prior session and up 0.9% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Demand is cooling in the labour market: Commonwealth Bank will cut 300 jobs amid an AI push and is setting out a retraining plan as job cuts loom. Financing is the long-run issue. Australia faces two decades of budget deficit, and UniSuper increased its hedging, judging the local currency undervalued.

Playbook ✓: Banks that are passing on rate rises are the near-term beneficiaries, since CBA and Westpac raised their own rates, but the job cuts make the sector a mixed trade. Prefer resource names while the AUD is up 2.11% over 20 sessions, and reduce housing-linked credit until the May-hike debate settles. The call changes if the monthly inflation gauge the RBA is studying confirms the hike path, or if the tariff drag takes the hike off the table.

Monetary & Activity: The central bank’s president is talking about where prices go next. Activity is soft: almost 10 thousand jobs disappeared in the latest monthly read, a drop the labour market has not seen in decades, and wage growth is the slowest in five years. Industry is weak, with production down and an unpleasant surprise for the market. The budget is weaker on revenue: income came in nearly 30 billion (zloty) below plan, while spending rose. The Finance Ministry summed up 2025 with income below plan and spending under control.

FX & Markets: USD/PLN is at 3.5748, up 0.28% in the prior session and 0.97% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). EUR/PLN is at 4.2189, up 0.34% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The iShares MSCI Poland ETF EPOL is at 37.95, up 0.56% over 20 sessions, and the Beta WIG20TR ETF is at 68.00 PLN, up 2.94% over five sessions and 1.66% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Among names, PKN is at 113.36 PLN, up 9.02% over 20 sessions; KGH is at 321.90 PLN, up 12.83% over five sessions but down 3.04% over 20; PEO is at 229.90 PLN, up 5.31%; CDR is at 240.00 PLN, down 9.71%; and ALE is at 28.30 PLN, down 6.92% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Rzeczpospolita says the WIG20 is under pressure as global markdowns and geopolitical tensions weigh, and Money.pl reports a red Tuesday with Modivo down more than 5% and banks dragging the index.

Companies: KGHM has a new chief executive, and the management is arguing for local content as a strategic advantage. Orlen acquired an interest in the Afrodite discovery on Norway’s continental shelf and is building a 25-million-boe North Sea portfolio. Orlen is also pushing billions of zloty of orders to Polish suppliers. Banks reported record profits despite the rate cuts, and the banking regulator is keeping a ‘close watch’ as banks buy Treasury bonds.

Security & New Development: Security rules are tightening. Cybersecurity rules now target non-NATO suppliers, and Chinese cars are banned from military bases. Money.pl says economists are unanimous in calling the SAFE defence loans a cold shower. GE Vernova says the deployment of its BWRX-300 small modular reactor in Poland has taken a major step forward, and nearly one million Ukrainian refugees are in Poland after four years of war.

Playbook ✓: Buy the rate-cut beneficiaries selectively and keep KGHM small until the new management’s first update. Prefer Orlen and PKN on the refining cycle, where PKN is up 9.02% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), and let the banks run only on fee-led earnings. ⚠ Divergence: the WIG20 total-return ETF is up 1.66% over 20 sessions and 2.94% over five, while Rzeczpospolita describes the WIG20 as under pressure, so the ETF and the index disagree on the tape.

Narrative: The software rout is the consensus concern and the rebound is fragile. Software stocks rebounded after Anthropic announced new partnerships, but investors are still looking for signs of a bottom. XLK closed at 140.32, up 1.3% in the prior session but down 3.94% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).
Reported: Workday forecast 2027 subscription revenue below estimates and its shares sank on weak revenue guidance. HP cut its fiscal-year expectations as memory prices drive up costs.

EPS Upside Watch: Nvidia reports later today, and the bar is set high: prediction markets put a beat at 95%, and the Reuters preview calls the print the AI market’s biggest test. NVDA closed at 192.85, up 4.26% over five sessions and 3.42% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Software is not the upside case until the guidance on AI demand is clearer.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The AI disruptors are carrying the rally. Anthropic’s partnership news lifted software, and Microsoft is up 1.18% in the prior session at 389.00, though it is still down 17.28% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Taleb’s warning to brace for software bankruptcies shows the bull case is not consensus.

Narrative: Advertising and capex are the debate. Amazon’s $200 billion AI spending plan has Wall Street asking one question, while Meta is down 4.92% over 20 sessions at 639.30 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). XLC closed at 116.16, down 1.37% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).
Reported: Snap’s direct revenue hit a $1 billion annualised run rate as subscribers topped 25 million. The number is the bull case that retail is using to argue for the stock.

EPS Upside Watch: The upside case is the subscription mix rather than the capex. Snap trades near $5 with 25 million paid subscribers and its bulls refuse to quit. Netflix is down 8.94% over 20 sessions at 78.04 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), so the group needs the ad and subscription mix to surprise.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Hyperscalers are buying power directly, which means the capex is moving into energy contracts. Google signed AES and Xcel supply deals to meet data-centre energy needs, so the spending that worries the group is also moving into the utilities.

Narrative: Private credit is the financials’ problem again. UBS sees private-credit defaults reaching 15% in its worst case, and Avenue Capital’s chief says the market has changed as the risk on software loans has risen. XLF closed at 50.98, down 2.34% over five sessions and 4.55% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

Reported: HSBC lifted its earnings target as annual profit dipped but beat estimates, and StanChart’s profit climbed. Scotiabank beat profit estimates, and OCBC’s profit rose on strong wealth fees, although Scotiabank’s earnings came as Canadian consumer credit weakened.

EPS Upside Watch: Canadian banks have a renewal cycle and valuation pressure ahead, and the Scotiabank profit beat is a rally that faces a test. The set-up is for trading and fee beats rather than loan growth, which the market has already started to price.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The banks beat and the group still sells off. Scotiabank and HSBC both beat estimates, yet the sector is down 4.55% over 20 sessions. The breaking signal is that the earnings are not what the sector is trading on; the private-credit mark is.

Narrative: Energy has the clearest geopolitical premium. Oil is at a seven-month high as tensions rise before US–Iran talks, and OilPrice calls it a seven-month high on the standoff. Brent closed at 70.77, up 7.9% over 20 sessions, and WTI at 65.63, up 8.25% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). XLE closed at 55.10, up 11.95% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

Reported: EOG Resources beat profit estimates on strong output and higher gas prices, and detailed a $6.5 billion 2026 capital plan. The capital plan is the discipline signal that the sector’s rally needs.

EPS Upside Watch: Goldman raised its Q4 oil price outlook on lower OECD stocks, which is a direct tailwind for upstream earnings into the next print. The EOG capital plan shows the producers are not chasing volume at this price, which supports the margin case.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The crude headlines conflict. Reuters says oil prices eased as Iran says it is prepared to take steps to reach a deal, while OilPrice reports a US crude stockpile surge weighing on prices. XLE is up 11.95% over 20 sessions even as the crude tape is mixed, so the premium is showing up in equities rather than in one clear crude direction.

Narrative: Industrial capex is the cyclical beneficiary. Caterpillar is up 20.81% over 20 sessions at 768.23 and GE is up 17.14% at 345.64 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). XLI closed at 176.98, up 1.23% in the prior session and 7.67% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). A Barron’s list names GE among five stocks that can win as AI shakes up the economy.

Reported: Kratos shares dropped after the drone maker beat estimates, and MTU Aero Engines shares fell after the outlook narrowly missed expectations. Spirit Airlines has a deal to emerge from bankruptcy with its lenders, and US airlines cancelled over 2,000 flights as the storm disruption continued.

EPS Upside Watch: Defence is the upside case: Morgan Stanley’s pick among defence stocks is set to rise another 20%. The aero-engine name shows the test is the outlook rather than the quarter, which is the same lesson as the consumer names.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Beats are being sold in the aerospace names. Kratos fell after its beat and MTU fell on its outlook. Industrial beats without a raised guide are being punished in the same tape that rewards the capex names, which is a discipline signal.

Narrative: Consumer discretionary is being squeezed by tariffs and by EV weakness. A dealership executive says automakers could start raising prices this year to offset tariffs, and Tesla’s Europe problem keeps getting worse. XLY closed at 116.74, up 1.52% in the prior session but down 4.56% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

Reported: Cava jumped 26% on a surprise same-store sales gain driven by menu prices, and Domino’s revenue rose on US same-store sales growth. Lucid widely missed earnings expectations, and Amer Sports dropped on a tepid outlook that raised cost concerns.

EPS Upside Watch: Lucid is the downgrade in the set-up: it sees lower production growth in 2026, to about 26,000. Home Depot’s beat is the cleaner read on the consumer, and the stock is up 1.99% in the prior session at 384.48 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Cava’s jump came from menu prices rather than from traffic. The market is paying for pricing power in restaurants, which is a warning about consumer volume, not a sign of a consumer recovery.

Narrative: Staples are expensive. A note says consumer staples have just got expensive in a way not seen in 25 years, and history sends a warning. XLP closed at 89.74, up 0.87% in the prior session and 8.41% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).
Reported: Nestlé beat on Q4 organic sales despite a profit drop, and plans to sell its ice cream business as fourth-quarter growth beat estimates. Both are defensive reads, not growth reads.
EPS Upside Watch: Herbalife is executing well but is no longer cheap, so any upside has to come from the guide rather than the valuation. The staples bar is the forward outlook, not the quarter.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Defence is being bought in a tape that is still falling for the consumer: XLP is up 8.41% over 20 sessions while XLY is down 4.56% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The market is paying for defence rather than for the consumer.

Narrative: Biotech M&A is supporting the sector. Gilead’s acquisition of Arcellx gave the target its best day ever, and the terms are being parsed. XLV closed at 157.87, down 0.42% in the prior session and 0.15% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). UnitedHealth is down 22.09% over 20 sessions at 273.95 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).
Reported: Fresenius Medical Care’s shares dropped after its outlook underwhelmed, while Ocular Therapeutix jumped after its AXPAXLI hit the SOL-1 Phase 3 endpoint in wet AMD.

EPS Upside Watch: Medtronic’s diabetes unit MiniMed is eyeing a $7.9 billion valuation in a US IPO, which tests the appetite for medtech listings. The EPS question for the parent is whether its guidance holds, not whether the unit lists.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Drug pricing risk is back in the conversation: Axios asks whether reality is the biggest challenge to Trump’s drug-price claims, while Eli Lilly is down 1.94% over 20 sessions at 1,042.15 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

Narrative: Materials are the metals trade, and the gold leg is consolidating. Gold slipped from a three-week high on dollar strength and profit-taking, while copper jumped on the hope of lower US levies. XLB closed at 53.36, up 6.66% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Gold is at 5,176.30, up 1.85% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

Reported: Ero Copper revealed a 24-year life and a $2 billion NPV for its Furnas project, and Hycroft Mining soared after a Sprott share purchase. The TSX hit a record, helped by the bull market for resource shares.

EPS Upside Watch: The copper set-up favours producers with volume. Freeport-McMoRan is up 10.97% over 20 sessions at 67.88 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), and the market is comparing it with SCCO as the better way to own the copper giants.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Gold is becoming a Hong Kong trading story: China eyes Hong Kong as its gold-trading hub, and gold has surpassed the dollar as a reserve asset in one headline. The bullish materials read is a policy story, while the near-term price signal is profit-taking.

Narrative: Real estate is leaning on the rates rally, which is stalling near 4% on the 10-year. XLRE closed at 43.73, up 6.09% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Deals are at work: GO Residential’s acquisition agreements raised its guidance, and OUE REIT’s Salesforce Tower stake is priced at A$357.2 million.

Reported: Lendlease REIT will acquire the remaining 30% of PLQ Mall and launched a $196.6 million rights issue. The Realty Income earnings preview is in the feed, and a fund that cut payouts 28% is a reminder that yield funds can reset.

EPS Upside Watch: The REIT upside case is about distributions. Trusts are positioned for higher DPUs if rates stay lower, which is the same rate-sensitivity the sector is trading on. A 10-year that stalls near 4% caps the rally.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Housing transactions and REITs disagree. Home sales fell by the most in four years in January and realtors call it a new housing crisis, yet REITs are rallying on the rate relief rather than on transaction data.

Narrative: Utility capex is the core. Dominion detailed a $65 billion five-year spending plan and ConEd eyes $38 billion through 2030. XLU closed at 47.20, up 1.11% in the prior session and 10.1% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). NextEra is up 11.95% over 20 sessions at 95.68 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

Reported: Constellation Energy reported full-year 2025 results, and Investor’s Business Daily says the nuclear leader topped earnings. Constellation closed at 312.64, up 6.41% in the prior session and 9.59% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

EPS Upside Watch: The demand side is in the Google power deals with AES and Xcel. The EPS upside is in contract flow rather than in the current run-rate, and the spending plans convert to rate-base growth only once the contracts are signed.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Power is now a constraint on AI rather than only a supply story. Data centres are hit by power delays and equipment shortages, and the boom is stalling in some markets. A utility’s capex plan is only as good as its interconnection queue.

Narrative: European autos are being pushed by two forces: a German export shock and Tesla’s Europe problem. German auto exports to China plunged by a third in 2025, and Tesla’s Europe problem keeps getting worse. The iShares STOXX Europe 600 Automobiles & Parts ETF closed at 46.29, up 1.95% in the prior session but only 2.95% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

Reported: Stellantis dealers in Europe are pushing for EU relief as sales lag. Mercedes, Nissan and Stellantis invested in the UK self-driving startup Wayve, and Wayve raised $1.2 billion from investors including Mercedes and Stellantis.
EPS Upside Watch: Stellantis is the case study. It faces a first annual loss after EV write-downs, and its upside depends on the US turnaround, with the new Jeep Cherokee leading the sales recovery.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Autonomy spending is rising in the same weeks that European car sales are falling. Wayve’s round is a valuation bet on the technology even as the volume data weaken, so the sector’s weakness is volume rather than technology spend.

Narrative: Semis are the AI-capex core. ASML has made an EUV breakthrough that plans to increase speed by 50% by 2030, and its systems sales are growing in double digits. SOXX closed at 362.04, up 1.46% in the prior session and 5.53% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). TSMC is up 15.94% over 20 sessions at 385.75 and ASML is up 5.98% at 1,497.80 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24).

Reported: Micron is riding the AI surge, but the memory trade could sour, and the stock-split speculation is in the feed. HP said the memory chip crunch will linger into next year and warned of a PC sales slump.

EPS Upside Watch: Nvidia’s report is the sector’s biggest set-up, and Reuters calls it the AI market’s biggest test amid competitive worries. The memory-chip shortage favours the memory makers over the PC makers, and Lenovo is signalling March price hikes on select devices.

⚡ Breaking Convention: AI supply constraints are now hurting the hardware buyers. Lenovo signals March price hikes and HP cuts its outlook on memory costs. The memory cycle that lifts the chipmakers is cutting into the buyers of their products, which cuts against a broad AI-hardware story.

Rewarded: Credible guidance and clean beats were paid in the latest week. Home Depot topped earnings estimates for the first time in a year, and its shares jumped 3.5% on the print. Cava jumped 26% on a surprise same-store sales gain. Ocular Therapeutix jumped after its Phase 3 endpoint, and Constellation Energy topped earnings. Herdez, Canadian Tire and Emera show the same pattern from the earlier week, where beats were rewarded.

Punished: Cautious outlooks get sold even after a beat. Workday sank on weak revenue guidance, and it forecast 2027 subscription revenue below estimates. Amer Sports dropped on a tepid outlook that raised cost concerns, and Fresenius Medical Care’s shares dropped after its outlook underwhelmed. Kratos fell even though it beat estimates, and MTU Aero Engines fell after its outlook narrowly missed. Lucid widely missed earnings expectations.

Pattern: The market is paying for the forward guide, again. Credible raises get the premium (Home Depot, Cava), and beats with a cautious outlook are sold (Workday, Kratos, MTU). Banks are a mixed case: Scotiabank beat estimates but the market is testing the rally, and HSBC’s profit dipped while still beating. Memory costs are the new margin risk for hardware, and HP cut its fiscal-year expectations on them. Scotiabank’s profit rose even as Canadian consumer credit weakened, so the market is rewarding fee and trading income over loan growth.

Attention into EPS: Nvidia’s report is the event of the day. Prediction markets put a beat at 95%, the expected move is in the preview, and Morgan Stanley reset its forecast before the print. Smaller previews are queued, including SoundHound, HP, Axon and Realty Income. Intuit’s stock crash has raised the stakes into its report.

Playbook: Own beats only where the guide rises, and sell beats where the guide is cut, particularly in hardware where memory costs are rising. For Nvidia, the guide is the test, not the quarter. Utilities whose plans rise on load remain the cleanest positive surprise path, as Dominion and ConEd show with their plan updates.

Attention Gap: Memory makers get the headlines while the hardware buyers absorb the cost. HP cut its fiscal-year expectations as memory prices drive up costs, and its warning that the crunch will linger into next year is not yet in most of the coverage. Lenovo is signalling March price hikes on select commercial devices.

Exposure & Risk: Name the instruments: Micron is the listed memory exposure, at 418.01 and up 7.43% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), while HP and Lenovo are the cost-squeezed side. The risk is that memory-cost pass-through fails, which would hit HP’s margin and its PC volume together.

Trigger to Watch: Lenovo’s March price increases are the first observable test. A pass-through to end-customers would make the hardware squeeze consensus, while a memory-price reversal would hand the margin back to the PC makers.

Attention Gap: The gold price is in every headline, but the reserve and hub story is less followed. Gold surpassed the US dollar as the top global reserve asset in one headline, and China is eyeing Hong Kong as a gold-trading hub to dominate the market. The Kitco item on China expanding its share and influence on the international gold market is part of the same story.

Exposure & Risk: Gold is at 5,176.30 and down 0.94% in the prior session, but up 1.85% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). SPDR gold ETF GLD is at 474.61, up 2.13% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The risk is that the hub plan stalls, or that profit-taking continues into the next leg of the gold rally.

Trigger to Watch: A formal Hong Kong gold-hub announcement, or a central-bank buying disclosure in the reserve data, would make this theme consensus. Until then the price moves on tariffs rather than on the reserve story.

Attention Gap: The Nikkei’s record high gets the headlines, and Goldman says the rally is not over. Less followed is that the BOJ board is being refilled with reflationists, which shifts the policy mix. The equity case rests on that, not on the record print alone.

Exposure & Risk: The Nikkei 225 closed at 57,321.09, up 6.45% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The currency risk is USD/JPY at 154.6, which is up 0.67% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). A weaker yen flatters exporters but squeezes importers and households.

Trigger to Watch: The BOJ’s next policy meeting, and any move on the yen after the board appointments, is the observable event. A hike signal would make the yen-hedged case a consensus trade; a yen rally would hurt the exporters first.

Attention Gap: Attention is on the RBA and on the mortgage borrower, not on the lenders. Commonwealth Bank and Westpac raised their own rates, which widens their margins while the central bank debates the next hike. The lenders are under-covered relative to the policy story.

Exposure & Risk: The listed exposure is CBA and Westpac, with the ASX 200 at 9,022.30 and up 0.9% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The risk is credit: CBA is cutting 300 jobs, and the rate rise squeezes households that are already under pressure.
Trigger to Watch: The monthly inflation gauge the RBA is studying is the trigger. A hot print confirms the hike path and keeps the margin tailwind; a soft one would bring the trade to an end.

Market Context: Bitcoin closed at 64,080.04 on the prior completed daily close, down 0.83% in that session and 12.24% over 20 sessions from 73,019.70 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Ether is at 1,852.97, down 13.55% over 20 sessions, and Solana at 79.04, down 14.12% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Bitcoin is on course for its worst month since the June 2022 collapse, having dipped below $63,000 before paring losses back above $64,000. The equity proxies are weaker: IBIT is down 26.42% over 20 sessions at 36.53, COIN is down 24.1% at 162.03 and MSTR is down 22.4% at 124.61 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Tom Lee calls the 50% drop a crypto squall rather than a winter, which is the bullish counter-narrative to the bear month.

New / Most Important: Institutional demand is weakening. US demand has turned negative for a record 40 days, and spot bitcoin ETFs have had five straight weeks of outflows, with February outflows deepening. The platforms are the pivot. Coinbase opened stock and ETF trading to all US users, and Meta is testing stablecoin payments and is planning a stablecoin comeback in the second half. Stripe’s tender offer values it at $159 billion, and RedotPay is weighing a $1 billion US IPO. Ether is still under pressure from Vitalik Buterin, who has sold 17K ETH in a month. The Ethereum Foundation has started a 70,000 ETH staking process to fund operations, a supply-side offset to the selling.

Playbook: Stay underweight bitcoin beta and express the platform narrative through the fee-earning names. Coinbase’s equity push is a diversification story, and the stock is down 24.1% over 20 sessions, which already prices much of the bear case (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The call changes if bitcoin reclaims its 20-session-earlier level of 73,019.70 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), or if the platforms’ stock-trading revenue shows up in the numbers. The downside marks in circulation include a $44K level from one trading note and a warning of a massive flush toward $55,000, so the position needs a hard stop rather than a level-based hope.

Global Liquidity: The dollar has lost some of its safe-haven status, and Asian currencies hit a 16-month high on the weak dollar and a stronger yuan. Hong Kong is pushing the offshore yuan with more borrowers. Warsh’s plan to slash the Fed’s balance sheet is the liquidity variable to watch, and Citigroup’s hedge-fund clients sold the dollar around the Supreme Court tariff ruling. Nikkei reports that the US Treasury Secretary initiated January’s yen-dollar rate check, which makes the liquidity lever a political one as well as a monetary one.

Rates & Dollar: The DXY is at 97.88, up 0.87% over 20 sessions and 0.74% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The curve is bull-flattening, with the 10-year at 4.04% and the 2-year at 3.43% (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-24). TLT is up 1.75% over 20 sessions at 89.90 and IEF is up 1.38% at 97.42 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Bloomberg reports the Treasury rally has stalled near 4%, while an ABC piece asks whether Treasuries could be a bubble about to burst. The 2-year is 13 bps lower over 20 sessions and the 10-year is 18 bps lower, so the belly is outperforming the long end (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-24).

Credit Check: Private credit is the credit signal. Default rates are rising and UBS sees defaults reaching 15% in its worst case. BofA has described the weakness concerns as misinformation, while a Bloomberg piece says the Blue Owl woes are clouding the private-credit outlook. Public credit has not followed: HYG is down 0.46% over 20 sessions at 80.81 and LQD is up 0.68% at 111.68 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Software loans are the pressure point: Avenue Capital says the risk on software loans has risen, and an investment chief says AI disruption is a threat to the booming private-credit market.

Equity & Fund Flows: Hedge funds crept back into tech after weeks of selling, yet BofA says US stocks drew the lowest share of global flows since 2020. US equity funds saw their largest weekly inflow in five weeks, and global equity funds drew the biggest inflow in five weeks, but Bloomberg says hedge funds sold most global equities since April. Retail leveraged ETF trading has surged. On the other side, the Saudi Wealth Fund unit plans to put more cash into private credit, which is a counterweight to the redemption pressure.

Portfolio Implication: Keep duration in the belly (IEF, up 1.38% over 20 sessions) and reduce private-credit and crypto beta. The dollar is only tactically weak, and the Asian currency rally is the one to own, while USD/CNY sits at 6.9080, 0.66% lower over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The two checkpoints are the Fed’s March rate call and the publication of the private-credit benchmarks. If private-credit funds keep selling assets below their stated value, the redemption channel is the one to hedge first, since it hits liquidity fastest.

What Is Priced: Prediction markets put a beat at 95%, and the expected move is already a topic. NVDA closed at 192.85, up 4.26% over five sessions and 3.42% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Morgan Stanley reset its forecast before the print, and the AMD and Meta deal has lifted the stock into the event. The bar is already high before the number is out.

Conditional Expression: If Nvidia beats and raises, the AI-capex leg holds and the position is long SOXX and NVDA. If it beats but only holds the guide, the skeptical read that the market is anxious about AI spending wins; sell the bounce and rotate into utilities (XLU) as the defensive hedge.

Risk: The AI-spending skepticism is already in the headlines, and the $200 billion spending question can overwhelm a beat if the capex guide is cautious. A beat that lifts the bar on guidance is the one outcome that turns the set-up negative.

What Is Priced: Oil is at a seven-month high as tensions rise before the US–Iran talks, and CNN asks why Trump is looking to strike again after saying Iran’s nuclear programme was obliterated. Brent is up 7.9% over 20 sessions at 70.77 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), so a premium is in the price.

Conditional Expression: If a deal emerges, and Iran says it is prepared to take steps toward one, the premium comes out: sell Brent and the energy names into the news and buy the belly as oil falls. If a limited strike comes, buy XLE and gold, with gold at 5,176.30 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24), and cut cyclicals.

Risk: The advisers are pushing an economy-first line, so the outcome is binary inside a short window. Place a stop on the no-deal, no-strike outcome, since talks can drag without a decision and oil will keep the premium.

What Is Priced: Goolsbee wants a hold because inflation is not good enough, Cook says AI may cause a short-term rise in unemployment, and Bostic says the Fed cannot offset structural unemployment. The 10-year is near 4%, and the 2-year is at 3.43% (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-24). Markets are therefore pricing the Fed as neither hiking nor cutting soon.

Conditional Expression: A labour print that confirms the hold keeps the curve bull-flattening: be long the belly (IEF) and short the front-end cut pricing. A weaker print brings a cut back: buy the 2-year and own defensive staples (XLP). Warsh’s balance-sheet plan is the risk that steepens the long end even if the front end rallies.

Risk: Waller does not expect AI to blow up the job market, which conflicts with Cook’s warning, so the Fed’s communication is mixed. A hawkish read on tariff-driven inflation would keep the front end sticky, and that breaks the bull-flattening pattern on the card.

What Is Priced: The new US levy is headline-confused: one report says it started at 10% with a plan to lift it to 15%, and another says it went in at 10%, not the 15% threatened. The EU has postponed its vote again and says it will accept no increase in US tariffs. Trump has warned that countries that play games with trade deals will face higher tariffs.

Conditional Expression: If the EU reschedules the vote and the US holds at 10%, buy the STOXX 600 and the German-exposed autos on a relief rally (SXAP). If the 15% levy is applied and the EU retaliates, sell the autos and rotate into XLP and XLU, which is where the defensive flows are going.

Risk: The trade policy has reversed within days before, so position sizing must assume the headline changes again. The rate, the vote and the retaliation are three separate checkpoints, and any one can move the set-up.

Catalyst & Thesis: Home Depot topped earnings estimates for the first time in a year, and its sales beat estimates on steady housing demand. The thesis is that the beat shows the repair-and-remodel demand is holding even as homeowners are weary of economic pressures.

Price Hurdle & Risk: HD closed at 384.48, up 1.99% in the prior session but 0.53% lower over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The hurdle is the 20-session drift, which the beat has not yet reversed. Risk is that housing transactions keep falling.
Trade Expression: Buy HD shares or a three-month call spread that caps the premium. Invalidate on a guide cut in the next housing print or on a fall back below the prior close.

Catalyst & Thesis: TSMC is speeding up its Taiwan expansion, with up to 10 fabs under construction or starting in 2026. The thesis is that the capacity roadmap converts into revenue over the next two years, and the AI-accelerator demand that the Nvidia print is testing is the same demand that TSMC serves.

Price Hurdle & Risk: TSM closed at 385.75, up 4.25% in the prior session and 15.94% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The stock is extended, so the hurdle is a pullback toward the 20-session-earlier level of 332.71 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Risk is that the rally already prices the fab build-out.
Trade Expression: Buy on pullbacks toward the mid-300s, or use SOXX as the lower-risk alternative. Invalidate on a tariff move aimed at Taiwan’s chip sector or a capex cut from the AI buyers.

Catalyst & Thesis: Workday forecast 2027 subscription revenue below estimates and its shares sank on weak revenue guidance. The thesis is that the AI-disruption debate is pricing the subscription base, and a weak forward guide proves the disruption is already in the numbers.

Price Hurdle & Risk: Workday is not in the card, so there is no price for the stock; the hurdle is the software rebound on partnership headlines. Risk is a wider relief rally in software if the Anthropic-led sentiment keeps lifting the group.
Trade Expression: Short Workday into any relief rally, or buy puts on the next rebound. Invalidate on a raised subscription guide or on a sustained rebound in the software group.

Catalyst & Thesis: Nvidia reports later today, with prediction markets at 95% for a beat. The AMD and Meta deal has lifted the stock into the print, and Wall Street skepticism over AI spending is in the headlines. The thesis is that the guide is the catalyst, and the stock is priced for a beat rather than a raise.

Price Hurdle & Risk: NVDA closed at 192.85, up 4.26% over five sessions and 3.42% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The hurdle is a beat that lifts the bar. Risk is that the AI-spending concern outweighs the beat.
Trade Expression: Mixed: stay flat through the print or buy an event straddle with a cap on premium. Invalidate on a guide that is in line, which would make the stock a sell into the next rally.

Catalyst & Thesis: HP cut its fiscal-year expectations as memory prices drive up costs, and said the memory chip crunch will linger into next year, warning of a PC sales slump. Lenovo is signalling March price hikes. The thesis is that the buyers absorb the cost, and the PC volume follows.

Price Hurdle & Risk: HP is not in the card, so there is no price for the stock. The hurdle is a pass-through of memory costs to end-customers, which would protect the margin. Risk is that the memory makers’ rally keeps supply tight.

Trade Expression: Short HP into the next PC pricing update, or buy the memory exposure through Micron, which is at 418.01 and up 7.43% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Invalidate on a pricing reset that passes the cost through.

Catalyst & Thesis: Tesla is down 11% in 2026 and Reddit is losing faith fast, while Tesla’s Europe problem keeps getting worse. The thesis is that the retail base that bought the dip is now the seller, and the European volume data confirm the demand gap.

Price Hurdle & Risk: TSLA closed at 409.38, up 2.39% in the prior session but 5.93% lower over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). The hurdle is a reversal of the European sales trend. Risk is a short squeeze if retail buyers return on any relief rally.

Trade Expression: Buy put spreads below the 20-session-earlier level of 435.20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24). Invalidate on a sustained European sales turn or a fresh retail-led rally that holds.
PayPal’s latest forum debate returns to execution and price, while Home Depot’s result, silver’s rebound and Tesla’s European challenge offer distinct operating and market tests.

Why Retail Is Here: PayPal is back in an explicitly identified retail discussion: 24/7 Wall St. reports Reddit divided over whether the shares at the price discussed are a steal or a trap. The attraction is a familiar payments company whose lower quote can look like an invitation to own an established business. The sceptical interpretation is that an apparently inexpensive share may still require difficult operating repair. The source describes a debate about PayPal on Reddit, not a view about Reddit Inc.'s own equity. That distinction leaves a useful company question: what must change in execution for the return available to a new PayPal shareholder to become attractive?

What Is Driving It: The operating context is the handover described in 24/7 Wall St.'s account of a new CEO inheriting an execution crisis. The latest discussion therefore has a concrete business hurdle behind the bargain label. A leadership change can alter priorities and accountability, while customers and merchants still need a reason to use and pay for the service. Examine how a plausible repair reaches revenue quality, costs and cash generation. A low quote may offer more room for improvement than an earlier price, but that room is valuable only if the company can use it. Do not value management change as though the commercial benefit has already been delivered.

The Social Signal: The split between 'steal' and 'trap' is the important attention signal. It makes the competing interpretations visible without establishing a market-wide count of buyers, sellers or posts. A recovery buyer can frame patience as an advantage over investors focused on the next disappointment. A cautious owner can see the same uncertainty as a reason to demand a larger margin of safety. Each interpretation should identify what evidence would change it. If every setback strengthens the bargain argument, or every improvement is dismissed as temporary, the discussion becomes an identity rather than an investment process. Borrow the question raised by the debate, rather than the confidence of its most emphatic participant.

Historical Analog: The mechanical analogy is the incumbent-platform turnaround. A business retains familiarity and distribution while the market debates whether its earlier advantages still support adequate shareholder returns. New leadership then offers a way to imagine repair before the operating evidence is complete. The similarity concerns the gap between a plausible plan and a delivered outcome, rather than a prediction that every established payments company follows the same path. Investors who remember a much higher share price can be especially vulnerable to anchoring. The useful reference is the earnings and cash generation the company can support from this point, not the quote at which another shareholder first became enthusiastic.

Smart Money View: A constructive professional view would ask whether modest improvements in execution can produce an acceptable return at the current entry. A cautious view would examine whether competition or customer behaviour requires more spending than the repair thesis assumes. Those are analytical questions rather than reported claims about a particular new initiative. Keep the scope of the forum source equally clear: a divided discussion is evidence of an argument, not proof that informed capital is accumulating the shares. An ordinary equity position can allow time for a repair; a leveraged option adds a deadline that the business may not meet even if the longer-term direction improves.

When the Narrative Breaks: The narrative weakens if the investment case continues to rely on the word 'cheap' while the execution assumptions remain unchanged. Set a limit on capital committed before adding to a declining position. Require company evidence that addresses the operating weakness, and reassess the valuation when that evidence changes. Reduce if patience has become an obligation to defend an earlier purchase rather than a choice supported by expected return. Revisit a bearish view if the specific repair becomes more credible at a price that still allows an ordinary outcome. The goal is an adequately priced business, not victory in a forum argument.

Why Retail Is Here: CNBC reports Home Depot beating estimates while project demand remains muted; the New York Times describes homeowners weary from economic pressures. The appealing interpretation is that the company can deliver a better result before a broad demand recovery. That is more precise than assuming every housing-linked business needs the same macro improvement.

Where It Breaks: Ask whether the operating result can persist without a rapid rebound in large projects. A familiar retail brand is not protection against paying too much for an earnings recovery. Reduce if the equity case requires demand to improve faster than the available evidence supports. Reconsider that view when company data strengthens the specific margin, demand or execution assumptions behind it.

Why Retail Is Here: Yahoo Finance describes SLV rising as Reddit bears wave the white flag. This is a fresh, attributed forum narrative about a rebound, rather than a verified measure of short positions being covered. The attraction is that a recent move can make an earlier sceptic fear missing the recovery.

Where It Breaks: SLV closed at 79.08, up 19.15% over five sessions but down 19.59% over 20 sessions. (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-24) The windows tell different parts of the story. Take partial profits if the rebound makes the position too large, and avoid increasing leverage simply because recent returns have improved. A futures contract is a different financing risk from an unleveraged ETF holding.

Why Retail Is Here: CNBC describes Tesla's European problem worsening. This is a new operating discussion alongside the earlier investor-ownership divide. A popular share can still face a regional business hurdle; enthusiasm by one investor group does not answer it.

Where It Breaks: Require evidence that improves the particular demand and profitability assumptions behind the position. Keep a long-term technology view distinct from a near-term business outcome in a specific market. Reduce if the thesis increasingly needs a distant possibility to offset each new operating concern. A familiar name should make the risk easier to identify rather than harder to reassess.

Market data: Yahoo Finance, prior completed sessions; Treasury curve: US Treasury daily par yields. Changes are price changes, not total returns. Currency sessions follow exchange-local dates; crypto observations include weekends.
